reference.source: Williams Obstetrics / Novak's Gynecology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: Stress urinary incontinence is involuntary leakage of urine on effort or exertion, such as coughing, sneezing, laughing, or physical activity, when abdominal pressure rises
It results from a weakened sphincter mechanism or poor support of the bladder neck and urethra, so that a rise in intra-abdominal pressure overcomes urethral closure
Key risk factors include vaginal childbirth, ageing and menopause, obesity, chronic cough or straining, and previous pelvic surgery
It must be distinguished from urgency incontinence (leakage with a sudden compelling desire to void); many women have a mixed picture with features of both
Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by a bladder diary, cough stress test, and exclusion of infection and significant post-void residual urine
First-line management is conservative: supervised pelvic floor muscle training, weight loss, treatment of chronic cough or constipation, and lifestyle measures
Adjuncts include continence pessaries or devices, and duloxetine may be considered in selected cases where surgery is unsuitable or declined

Surgical options for persistent bothersome stress incontinence include mid-urethral slings, colposuspension, and urethral bulking agents, chosen according to patient factors and shared decision-making
Urodynamic testing is reserved for complex, mixed, or recurrent cases or before surgery where the diagnosis is uncertain, rather than being routine
reference.pathophysiology: Continence during exertion depends on adequate urethral closure pressure and on the bladder neck and urethra being well supported so that rises in abdominal pressure are transmitted equally to the bladder and proximal urethra. Two overlapping mechanisms cause stress incontinence: urethral hypermobility, in which weakened pelvic floor and endopelvic fascial support (often after childbirth or with ageing) allows the bladder neck to descend and the pressure transmission to become unequal; and intrinsic sphincter deficiency, in which the urethral closure mechanism itself is weakened, for example after surgery, radiation, or oestrogen deficiency. In either case a cough or exertion transiently raises bladder pressure above urethral resistance and urine escapes.
additionalDifferentials: Urinary tract infection causing transient symptoms
Functional incontinence from mobility or cognitive impairment
additionalInvestigations: Bladder (frequency-volume) diary to characterise the pattern of leakage
Cough stress test to demonstrate leakage with raised abdominal pressure
Urinalysis and culture to exclude infection
Post-void residual measurement to exclude incomplete emptying
Pad testing to quantify leakage where useful
Urodynamic studies in complex, mixed, recurrent, or pre-surgical cases
redFlags: Visible haematuria requiring exclusion of urinary tract malignancy
Significant post-void residual or voiding difficulty indicating retention with overflow
New neurological symptoms suggesting a neurological cause
Recurrent urinary infections or pain warranting further evaluation
reference.prognosis: Stress incontinence is not life-threatening but can substantially impair quality of life. Many women improve significantly with conservative measures, particularly sustained pelvic floor muscle training and weight loss. Surgical procedures offer high rates of symptom improvement in appropriately selected patients, though some experience recurrence or complications, so treatment is individualised through shared decision-making.
pitfalls: Labelling all incontinence as stress type without identifying a mixed or urgency component
Proceeding to surgery without a trial of conservative therapy or without clarifying the diagnosis
Missing overflow incontinence by not checking post-void residual
Overlooking a fistula in a patient with continuous leakage, especially after surgery or childbirth
Attributing symptoms to stress incontinence when haematuria or infection needs investigation
